title: Gently Johnny: Folk Horror & the Wicker Man Underground
author: Claudette
description: Britain's pagan underbelly 1968-73: Comus, Fairport, Anne Briggs, the Wicker Man OST — and the Drag City revivalists who carried the torch.

essay:
Every folk revival has a bright side and a dark side. In late-60s Britain the bright side was the pastoral hippie dream — the Incredible String Band's cosmic whimsy, Pentangle's jazz-folk, Vashti Bunyan's wagon songs. The dark side was the ancient repertoire underneath it: Child Ballads about elf knights and human sacrifice, murder ballads about the Red Barn, warnings about maidens losing their thyme. This playlist is the dark side, from its roots to its revival.

The whole scene was one room. Producer Joe Boyd (Witchseason) and arranger Robert Kirby (Nick Drake's string arranger) supervised the same musicians drifting between each other's records — Robin Williamson, Dave Swarbrick, Simon Nicol, Danny Thompson. The transmission chain is the theme in miniature: Anne Briggs taught 'Blackwaterside' to Bert Jansch, who cut it on Jack Orion (1966); Jimmy Page turned it into 'Black Mountain Side' on Led Zeppelin I (1969), uncredited — folk as open source, for better and worse. Meanwhile Fairport Convention invented British folk-rock in 1969 (Unhalfbricking, Liege & Lief), survived the motorway crash that killed drummer Martin Lamble, and Sandy Denny left for a solo career and one immortal cameo on Zeppelin's 'The Battle of Evermore.' The darkest branch flowered 1970–72: Trees, Comus (regulars at David Bowie's Arts Lab), Mellow Candle (two Irish teenagers), Shirley Collins' No Roses, Roy Harper's Stormcock with Jimmy Page credited as 'S. Flavius Mercurius.'

The Wicker Man (1973) sealed the genre: an American theater composer, Paul Giovanni, writing a pagan-sounding folk score for Robin Hardy's film so convincing it's still folk horror's definitive sound — 'Willow's Song,' 'Gently Johnny' (sung by Giovanni himself in the pub scene), the Middle English 'Sumer Is Icumen In' finale. The soundtrack went unreleased until Trunk Records' mono 1998 edition; the stereo 2002 Silva Screen version restored 'Gently Johnny.' Then the 2000s rediscovered the whole underground. Vashti Bunyan returned after a 30-year silence; Joanna Newsom's homemade EP reached Will Oldham, who passed it to Drag City; Espers released II on Drag City; and the line runs forward to Jessica Pratt and Meg Baird on Drag City today. Cat Power covered Sandy Denny's 'Who Knows Where the Time Goes' on The Covers Record (2000) — the direct line into the modern indie canon. Seventeen tracks, from the root of the tree to its newest leaves.
